newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Crude prices in Asia slump after Iraqi stand down.
newsitem.headline: Crude prices in Asia slump after Iraqi stand down.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia fell sharply on Monday as traders cashed in their profits after Iraq appeared to have defused Gulf tensions with the United States.
"I would think the rally is over, barring fresh developments," said one crude oil trader. "But with this market, you should never be surprised."
Benchmark North Sea Brent November futures prices slumped 64 cents per barrel on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) to end at $22.49.
The slide continued in London, where Brent futures are also traded. November Brent last traded at $22.38 in early evening Asia time.
On Thursday, at the height of the tension following Iraq's firing of missiles at U.S. warplanes, November Brent had peaked at $23.60.
New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) October crude oil futures, another benchmark, were last traded in Asian hours at $24.00 per barrel, down from Thursday's $25.35 peak.
Iraq said late on Friday it would no longer fire anti-aircraft missiles at U.S. and allied warplanes enforcing no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq.

The announcement somewhat eased tensions that had continued for two weeks since U.S. bombers and warships fired 44 missiles at Iraqi targets in retaliation for Iraq's incursion into northern Kurdish areas of the country.
The United States said further attacks on Iraq were possible, but at the same time said it would not overreact.

The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Madeleine Albright, said in a television interview: "It looks as though Saddam Hussein is not going to do anything else... I think we're going to keep watching the whole issue very, very carefully."
Crude oil prices started to ease in London late on Friday. Brent slipped four cents per barrel to $23.13, but NYMEX crude shed 49 cents to $24.51.

"I would think that what Iraq has said shows they are backing down a bit. From a fundamental perspective, I would say that oil prices at $24 and $25 per barrel are a bit high," one crude trader said on Monday.
He said the price on NYMEX for October could slide to $22.50 per barrel before the sell off stopped.
Brokerage Credit Lyonnais Rouse Ltd had a less bearish view.
"Without news, the market is looking overbought technically and could fall 50 cents before finding support," it said.

Iraq's incursion into the north resulted in the U.N. freezing an oil-for-food deal that would have let Baghdad sell oil for the first time since the Gulf War and raise $2 billion for food and humanitarian goods.
Analysts said they believed the deal would not be revived until 1997, or at least until after the U.S. presidential election in November.
Iraq had been expected to start selling 700,000 barrels of crude per day as early as this month and put downward pressure on prices.
One trader said if Iraq were allowed to sell oil sooner than the market expected, such as before the end of the year, prices could drop $2 or $3 per barrel because of the "psychological impact."
